title: Sending Secrets Without Sharing a Secret First

sources.title: RFC 9180 — Hybrid Public Key Encryption
sources.notes: Introduces hybrid asymmetric/symmetric designs and KEM/KDF/AEAD composition. Episode distinguishes its conceptual wrapped-key teaching model from exact HPKE.

sources.title: RFC 5116 — An Interface and Algorithms for Authenticated Encryption
sources.notes: AEAD confidentiality/integrity interface, authentication failure, and scheme-specific nonce requirements.

sources.title: RFC 8446 — TLS 1.3
sources.notes: TLS1.3 uses authenticated key establishment and AEAD; static RSA key transport removed. Used to distinguish the simplified diagram from modern TLS.

sections.title: A secret on a public network
sections.narration: Alice wants to send Bob a private message, but Eve can observe their network traffic. Sending the message openly reveals its contents. Sending a shared password openly seems to recreate the same problem. We will separate encryption from authentication and see how symmetric and public-key techniques can cooperate in one simplified design.
sections.takeaway: A public network needs more than a promise that nobody is listening.

sections.title: Plaintext becomes ciphertext
sections.narration: Plaintext is the original information. An encryption algorithm takes plaintext and a key to produce ciphertext, which should conceal the information from someone without the necessary secret. Decryption reverses that transformation with the appropriate key. Our scrambled letters are visual symbols, not the output of an implemented or secure encryption algorithm.
bullets: Illustrated symbols are not real crypto
sections.takeaway: Encryption conceals content through a keyed transformation.

sections.title: The algorithm can be public
sections.narration: A well-designed cryptographic system should not depend on hiding how the algorithm works. Algorithms can be published and studied, while security depends on appropriate secret keys and the scheme’s assumptions. This is different from inventing a private substitution rule and hoping nobody guesses it. Public analysis helps reveal weaknesses before an attacker does.
bullets: Secrecy of design is not a foundation
sections.takeaway: Protect the key rather than relying on an unknown algorithm.

sections.title: Symmetric encryption uses a shared secret
sections.narration: With symmetric encryption, Alice and Bob possess the same secret key, or closely related secret material within the chosen scheme. Alice encrypts and Bob decrypts using that shared secret. Symmetric algorithms are suitable for processing substantial data efficiently. Eve may know the algorithm and see the ciphertext while still lacking the key.
sections.takeaway: A symmetric key must remain secret from unauthorized parties.

sections.title: A key is not simply a memorable password
sections.narration: A cryptographic key needs the length and unpredictability required by its algorithm. A human password is often much easier to guess. Password-based systems use dedicated derivation mechanisms rather than treating a short word as an ideal random key. This episode’s key icons represent properly generated key material, not advice to invent one manually.
sections.takeaway: Use appropriate key generation rather than a memorable homemade key.

sections.title: The key-distribution problem
sections.narration: Our shared-key diagram hides an important question: how did Alice and Bob obtain the same secret? If Alice sends that key in plaintext across the observed channel, Eve can capture it and decrypt subsequent messages. Symmetric encryption is not broken here; its required secret was exposed before the protection could help.
bullets: Sending K openly reveals the secret
sections.takeaway: Secure encryption still needs a sound way to establish or distribute keys.

sections.title: Give Bob a pair of keys
sections.narration: Public-key encryption introduces a related pair: Bob’s public key can be distributed, while Bob keeps his private key secret. In an appropriate encryption scheme, Alice can protect information using the public key so that Bob can recover it with his private key. The private key is not derived from the public key by an easy reversal.
sections.takeaway: A public/private key pair assigns different capabilities to each key.

sections.title: Publish the encryption key
sections.narration: Bob can publish his public encryption key without giving every observer the ability to decrypt messages intended for him. That asymmetry is the useful idea. However, being public does not mean the key is automatically trustworthy. Alice must still establish that the public key she received really belongs to Bob.
bullets: Public also does not mean trusted
sections.takeaway: Public-key distribution and public-key authentication are different problems.

sections.title: Encrypt to Bob’s public key
sections.narration: Alice uses Bob’s authenticated public key with a suitable public-key encryption scheme. Eve sees the resulting ciphertext, but possession of the public key alone does not supply Bob’s decryption capability. We are illustrating a security goal under a scheme’s assumptions, not claiming that every algorithm labeled public-key encryption is safe for arbitrary use.
bullets: Observing PK_B does not reveal SK_B
sections.takeaway: Use a suitable scheme and the intended recipient’s authenticated public key.

sections.title: Decrypt with the private key
sections.narration: Bob uses his private key to recover the protected information. He must safeguard that key because its compromise can expose information protected for it, depending on the protocol and its forward-secrecy properties. A private key should not appear in the transmitted envelope. Our animation keeps it beside Bob throughout the exchange.
bullets: The private key is not transmitted
sections.takeaway: Protecting private keys is part of protecting the communication.

sections.title: Why not encrypt every file this way?
sections.narration: Public-key operations are generally more costly and constrained than symmetric bulk encryption. Practical systems therefore combine techniques rather than encrypting an entire large file directly with a simple public-key primitive. The goal is to gain public-key key-management advantages while keeping efficient symmetric protection for the actual application data.
sections.takeaway: Hybrid designs combine complementary capabilities.

sections.title: Generate a fresh session key
sections.narration: For our simplified hybrid example, Alice generates a fresh random symmetric session key K. This key will protect the message data for the illustrated exchange. Freshness limits inappropriate key reuse, but it is not a substitute for the scheme’s other requirements. Alice must also follow rules for nonces, authentication, and secure key handling.
bullets: Generate fresh random session key K
sections.takeaway: A hybrid example begins with appropriate session key material.

sections.title: Protect the data with the session key
sections.narration: Alice protects the message using an authenticated symmetric encryption scheme and K. The resulting package includes ciphertext and an authentication tag, along with any required nonce and associated metadata. The exact format depends on the scheme. The key remains separate from this data package until the public-key protection step.
sections.takeaway: Authenticated symmetric encryption protects the bulk message.

sections.title: Protect the session key for Bob
sections.narration: In this teaching model, Alice encrypts the small session key using Bob’s authenticated public encryption key. Eve can observe the protected session key without learning K under the scheme’s security assumptions. This is a conceptual key-transport example. Modern hybrid standards can instead use encapsulation and derivation, with additional details beyond this diagram.
bullets: PK_B protects the small session key
This is a simplified key-transport model
sections.takeaway: Protect the session key separately from the bulk ciphertext.

sections.title: Send the two protected pieces
sections.narration: Alice transmits the protected session-key material and the authenticated ciphertext package. Eve can copy both, so the design must remain secure despite observation. Encryption does not conceal every aspect of traffic: endpoints, approximate message sizes, and timing may still be visible. Content confidentiality should not be confused with complete anonymity.
bullets: Send protected key material and data
sections.takeaway: Ciphertext can conceal content while revealing other communication patterns.

sections.title: Bob recovers the key, then the message
sections.narration: Bob first uses his private key to recover K in our simplified key-transport diagram. He then uses K to authenticate and decrypt the data package. Verification failure means the package must be rejected rather than treated as valid plaintext. The asymmetric and symmetric steps have different responsibilities within the same workflow.
bullets: K authenticates and decrypts the data
sections.takeaway: A hybrid receiver verifies the protected data before accepting its contents.

sections.title: Secrecy alone does not detect tampering
sections.narration: Confidentiality asks whether an observer can learn the message. Integrity asks whether unauthorized changes can be detected. Encryption without an appropriate integrity mechanism may fail to detect malicious modification. That is why our example uses authenticated encryption rather than presenting arbitrary ciphertext as automatically tamper-proof. These properties need deliberate mechanisms.
sections.takeaway: Encryption and integrity are related but distinct security goals.

sections.title: An authentication tag checks the package
sections.narration: An authenticated encryption scheme produces a tag that the receiver verifies using the relevant secret and inputs. Changing protected ciphertext or authenticated metadata should cause verification to fail, subject to the scheme’s guarantees. A tag is not simply an unkeyed checksum. Anyone can recompute a basic checksum after altering a message.
bullets: A checksum is not a keyed authenticator
sections.takeaway: Authenticated encryption detects invalid protected packages.

sections.title: Do not reuse nonces carelessly
sections.narration: Many authenticated encryption schemes require nonce uniqueness for a given key. Reusing a nonce can seriously compromise confidentiality or authenticity, with consequences depending on the scheme. A nonce is not necessarily secret, and it is not a replacement for the key. Real software must enforce the selected scheme’s exact requirements.
bullets: A nonce is separate from the key
sections.takeaway: Correct nonce handling is essential to secure authenticated encryption.

sections.title: A substituted public key changes everything
sections.narration: Suppose Eve replaces Bob’s public key with her own before Alice receives it. Alice might encrypt to Eve while believing she is addressing Bob. Encryption can work perfectly and still protect the message for the wrong recipient. Certificates, trusted key fingerprints, or other authenticated distribution mechanisms address this identity-binding problem.
sections.takeaway: A public key is useful only with an appropriate trust decision.

sections.title: Confidentiality is not a sender’s signature
sections.narration: Anyone who has Bob’s public encryption key can potentially create a message encrypted for Bob. Successful decryption therefore does not, by itself, identify Alice as the sender. Digital signatures provide a different capability using appropriate signing and verification schemes. Do not describe signing as merely encrypting a whole message with a private key.
bullets: Encrypting for Bob does not identify Alice
sections.takeaway: Recipient confidentiality does not automatically authenticate the sender.

sections.title: How this differs from modern TLS
sections.narration: The public-key-wrapped session key illustrates hybrid thinking, not the TLS 1.3 handshake. TLS 1.3 commonly authenticates an ephemeral key exchange, derives traffic keys, and protects records with authenticated encryption. It removed static RSA key transport. Modern protocols add identity checks, transcript binding, replay protections, and other details omitted from our teaching diagram.
sections.takeaway: Use the hybrid idea to understand protocols without confusing their mechanisms.

sections.title: Use established cryptographic protocols
sections.narration: These pictures explain responsibilities, not instructions to design a new encryption format. Real applications should use maintained cryptographic libraries and established protocols, including correct certificate validation and secure randomness. A clever-looking padlock animation cannot demonstrate cryptographic strength. Security depends on algorithms, parameters, implementation, key management, and the surrounding protocol together.
bullets: A visual analogy is not a security proof
sections.takeaway: A sound implementation must preserve the whole protocol’s security assumptions.

sections.title: Solve the secrecy puzzle
sections.narration: Symmetric encryption efficiently protects data when endpoints share suitable secret material. Public-key techniques help establish or protect that material without first sending a plaintext shared key. Authenticated keys, integrity checks, and correct nonce handling remain essential. Alice can communicate privately over an observable channel only when these complementary responsibilities fit together correctly.
bullets: Combine key setup and data protection
sections.takeaway: Secure communication combines confidentiality, integrity, and sound key handling.
